19980-a-joy-for-ever-and-its-price-in-th:
John Ruskin delivered A Joy For Ever at Manchester in 1857. Its full theme is the political economy of art. Ruskin finds one trait most notable in the age. We hold poverty in a just and wholesome contempt, he repeats. That contempt, he argues, shapes how art gets bought and valued. Two lectures, given July 10 and 13, make the book. Ruskin asks what beauty costs and who pays.

Ruskin was Victorian England's greatest art critic and a fierce social thinker. These lectures turn criticism toward wages, prices, and public taste. He insists art's value is moral before it is monetary. The talks scandalized Manchester's merchant audience pleasantly little at first. Later readers found them prophetic of arts funding debates. It is Ruskin the reformer in full voice.
20121-lone-star-planet:
Lone Star Planet is a science fiction tale set on a world run much like old Texas. It opens in the office of a Secretary of State on Earth. Ghopal Singh, dark-faced and grey-haired, meets a guest at his desk. Rudolf Klüng, of the Department of Aggression, stands by in black.

From Earth, the action moves to a planet that prizes guns and beef. Diplomats there must learn local ways fast or fail badly. The tale mixes satire, western codes, and space travel in one romp. Readers get a sharp, funny look at power, pride, and frontier law.
20147-rip-foster-rides-the-gray-planet:
Blake Savage wrote Rip Foster Rides the Gray Planet, a space tale for young readers. An officer of the Special Order Squadrons stands his men at ease. He warns that duty calls for a farewell speech from him. He means to make that speech if it kills them all, he jokes.

Rip Foster serves with a space force modeled on old army ways. Rockets, gray planets, and alien worlds fill his missions with risk. Books like this one fed the space dreams of postwar boys. Readers get brisk action, team spirit, and the thrill of early space fiction.
20212-police-your-planet:
Police Your Planet, from 1956, is a science fiction tale set on Mars. A man looks back at his rocket, still pointing skyward behind him. Ahead sprawls Marsport, a mess of slums beyond the air dome. The dome holds breathable air over the city's central part alone.

Law on such a frontier world is rough, bought, and badly bent. An honest man sent to police it faces graft at every turn. The tale mixes crime, politics, and space colony grit. Readers get a hard, fast dose of 1950s pulp science fiction.
20238-the-great-amulet:
Maud Diver wrote The Great Amulet, a novel set among the British in India. All the wedding preliminaries are over as one bright scene opens. A cheerful breakfast of cold chicken, iced cake, and champagne follows. It is served in Maurice's plain rooms over a pastry-cook's shop.

Diver wrote many novels of Anglo-Indian life, love, and duty. Her couples face heat, distance, caste, and the rules of two worlds. The great amulet of the title hints at charm, faith, and fate. Readers get romance rooted in the daily life of British India.
20400-on-the-heels-of-de-wet:
On the Heels of De Wet recounts the hunt for the Boer general Christiaan de Wet during the South African war. The writer, who calls himself the Intelligence Officer, served with the British forces chasing him. De Wet's raids and escapes made him the war's most elusive enemy.

The author admits that a few criticisms crept into his text. He asks readers to recall that regimental officers had suffered in silence for the sins of others. The book mixes campaign narrative with sharp views on how the war was run, from a man who rode in the pursuit.
20737-madge-morton-s-secret:
Amy D. V. Chalmers published Madge Morton's Secret in 1914, opening on a bright September morning. An old Virginia orchard smells of ripe apples, and a press still drips with cider. No one is in sight but one girl, alone among the trees.

That calm start soon gives way to the secret of the title. Madge must guard what she knows while life presses in around her. Chalmers writes for girls who liked feeling, loyalty, and a touch of mystery. The Virginia setting, with its orchards and old homes, gives the tale a warm, rooted feel throughout.
20739-rebels-of-the-red-planet:
Charles L. Fontenay spent his career in newspaper work, starting in 1936 with three papers and the Associated Press. He later worked as rewrite man for The Nashville Tennessean. That newsman's speed shows in Rebels of the Red Planet, his tale of Mars.

Fontenay sets revolt on a harsh red world ruled from Earth. Fast scenes, plain talk, and sudden turns keep the plot moving. The book came from the pulp age of science fiction, when Mars still felt close and strange. Readers get a brisk adventure with a reporter's eye for who holds power and who pays for it.
21270-five-hundred-dollars-or-jacob-marl:
Horatio Alger Jr. opens in the village of Lakeville, where an elderly traveller with bronzed features and a stout cane returns after twenty years away. He wonders aloud whether the two families near to him will welcome him. A polite boy of fifteen, in coarse clothes that show narrow means, stops to answer his questions.

The stranger is Jacob Marlowe, and his secret, tied to five hundred dollars, drives the tale. The boy's family, by contrast, is poor and honest, the usual Alger pattern. Alger wrote dozens of such stories of boys rising by pluck and honesty. A fine house down the street, with two horses and handsome carriages, marks what money looks like in Lakeville.
21556-travels-and-adventures-of-monsieur:
Monsieur Violet's father follows his exiled king to Edinburgh in Captain Marryat's tale of 1843. The boy, then nine, leaves France for good at his father's side. In time the road leads far from Scotland, into the wilds of North America.

Marryat drew much of the book from his own American visit, whose diary appeared in 1839. Trappers, Indigenous peoples, and frontier hunts crowd Violet's travels. The book was Marryat's twentieth, written with his usual speed and invention. Readers get a French hero's view of the prairies, forests, and rivers of the young continent.
22036-recollections-of-forty-years-in-th:
John Sherman spent forty years at the centre of American public life. He served in the House, the Senate, and the Cabinet, and his Recollections of that career appeared in 1895. The book opens with the Sherman family's Saxon roots along the Rhine. It then follows his own rise from Ohio lawyer to national figure.

Sherman helped finance the Union during the Civil War from the Senate. Later he ran the Treasury and gave his name to the Antitrust Act of 1890. His memoir argues his side of old fights over money and trusts. Historians still mine it for an insider's view of Reconstruction-era politics.

Hudson Bay, with its ice, trading posts, and northern waters, gave him a stern setting for this outing.

catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-stephen-of: St. Stephen of Muret was the founder of Grandmont. This entry traces his hermits, his Limousin, and his fame. The solitary of the French hills: his new order crowned Grandmont in the 1070s' Limousin in the hills of the Ambazac.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-thomas-bec: St. Thomas Becket was the martyr archbishop. This long entry examines his Henry, his Canterbury, and his cult. The saint of the English church: his martyr's blood sealed Canterbury in the 1170 of the knights in the cathedral of the choir.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-thomas-gar: St. Thomas Garnet was the Jesuit martyr. This entry traces his Tyburn, his constancy, and his crown. The nephew of the Gunpowder priest: his martyr's blood sealed Tyburn in the 1608 of the mission in the city of the Thames.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-theodoret: Theodoret was the bishop of Cyrus. This very long entry examines his 400s, his history, and his Christology. The historian of the Eastern church: his church history crowned Cyrus in the 400s of the Theodosius in the very old east.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-marie-: Gousset was the cardinal of Reims. This long entry examines his 1800s, his theology, and his see. The archbishop of the coronation city: his proud Reims crowned Champagne in the 1840s of the Louis-Philippe in the truly very old throne.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-somers: Somerset was the martyr of the west. This entry traces his 1500s, his seminary, and his death. The priest of the English mission: his brave death crowned the west in the 1580s of the mission in the very old hills.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tibet: Tibet is the roof of the missions. This very long entry examines its Lhasa, its lamas, and its Capuchins. The land of the forbidden plateau: their forbidden Lhasa crowned the Himalayas in the 1700s of the Capuchins in the mission.
caught-in-the-net: Caught in the Net, Émile Gaboriau's detective novel. The trapped criminal. This book preserves that mystery. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
diary-of-a-pedestrian-in-cashmere-and-th: This diary records a bold walk through Cashmere and Thibet. The traveler crosses high passes and strange valleys on foot. Mountain peoples and customs fill the pages. A rare Victorian glimpse of the roof of the world.
doe-osti-17198190-uncertainty-and-sensit: GDSA's uncertainty methods got their FY2026 write-up, and this report covers sensitivity analysis applications. The pages detail the framework. The modelers get their toolkit. The year was FY2026. The toolkit was framework. The framework was GDSA. The toolkit was modeling.
doe-osti-1764912-region-specific-merchan: Hydrogen for sale, region by region, got its DOE market study, and this report prices electrolytic production. The pages break down the local numbers. The planners get their map. The map was regional. The production was electrolytic. The study was DOE's.
doe-osti-2589169-defining-a-platform-app: Solid state transformers got their platform approach, and this DOE report defines data-driven business models. The pages detail the market participation. The grid innovators get their playbook. The models were data-driven. The models were business. The innovators got playbooks.
doe-osti-2589619-uncertainty-and-sensiti: Measuring doubt in waste repository models got its DOE playbook, and this FY2025 report sharpens the methods. The pages detail the sensitivity tools. The modelers get their guide. The doubt was uncertainty. The tools were sensitivity. The guide was modeler.
doe-osti-3002178-application-of-raman-sp: Raman spectroscopy got applied to uranium, and this DOE text measures ADUN solution content. The pages detail the findings. The chemists get their method. The solution was ADUN. The method was chemist. The content was uranium. The method was Raman.
doe-osti-3005574-optimization-of-scintil: X-ray cameras that glow got their DOE tune-up, and this text sharpens the MeV pictures. The pages detail the detector tweaks. The diagnosticians get their tool. The glow was scintillation. The tweaks were detector. The tune-up was DOE's.
doe-osti-3008148-determination-of-scale-: AGHCF metallography got its scale bar, and this DOE text determines the data measure. The pages detail the findings. The materials folks get their calibration. The data were metallography. The calibration was material. The bar was scale. The metallography was AGHCF.
doe-osti-3008387-2023-annual-explosives-: Explosives inventory got completed, and this DOE text covers the 2023 annual count. The pages detail the findings. The safety folks get their record. The year was 2023. The record was safety. The count was annual. The inventory was explosives. The record was DOE's.
doe-osti-3025065-carbon-neutral-steel-pr: Steel got methane-pyrolyzed, and this DOE final produces carbon-neutral iron. The pages detail the report findings. The industry folks get their closeout. The iron was direct reduced. The closeout was industry. The pyrolysis were methane. The reduced were direct.
doe-osti-3380293-multilayer-membrane-ele: MESPA got PEM-assembled, and this DOE text covers membrane electrode stacks. The pages detail the multilayer findings. The engineers get their data. The assembly was facile. The data were engineer. The MESPA were gasket. The PEM were stacks. The facile were assembly.
doe-osti-3394856-leveraging-solar-therma: Brewing got solar-leveraged, and this DOE text covers net-zero thermal energy. The pages detail the leveraging findings. The energy folks get their data. The brewing was net-zero. The data were energy. The zero were net. The brewing were thermal.
doe-osti-3398694-role-of-neutrals-versus: Pedestals got neutral-rolled, and this DOE final covers density structures. The pages detail the technical findings. The physicists get their closeout. The transport was versus. The closeout was physicist. The pedestal were density. The versus were transport. The density were structures.
essays-on-paul-bourget: Mark Twain's essays on Paul Bourget: the French critic answered. Twain defends American manners. Sharp and funny. The humorist as critic, twain answers the French critic with wit, american manners defended, sharp and funny, Twain the critic.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FBISocietyofFor: An article called Hoover's Loyal Legion profiles the Society of Former Special Agents of the FBI, the organization of men who once served under J. Edgar Hoover. The nickname in the title is the point: loyalty to the old director outlasted his tenure. The surviving record gives the subject and title but no author or date, so the piece stands as an undated portrait of the Bureau's alumni society.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-RifleandBullet_:
Remington Arms Company issued this Remington-Peters catalog for 1971. It lists the company's sporting firearms and ammunition for that year. Shotguns and rifles are presented with their models and prices. High-velocity ammunition gets its own place in the line. The catalog is a sales book, made for dealers and sportsmen planning a season.

A manufacturer's catalog fixes a year's products exactly: names, gauges, barrel lengths, and prices in print. Gun catalogs sit in assassination files because the Oswald rifle was a mail-order product of the same world. This one is valuable on its own terms. It preserves Remington's 1971 line entire, the sporting market as the maker chose to present it.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_cuba_Cub:
On December 17, 2014, Presidents Barack Obama and Raúl Castro announced a breakthrough in United States-Cuba relations. Behind that public moment lay years of secret contacts. Peter Kornbluh edited this major collection, announced in December 2017 near the third anniversary of that date.

The documents chart the history of secret communications between the two governments. Back channels let enemies talk when open diplomacy is frozen, and this set preserves how those talks worked in practice. It is a useful record for anyone studying how long-hostile states begin, quietly, to change course.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_cuba_Sav:
After the Bay of Pigs invasion failed, more than a thousand invaders sat in Cuban prisons. Getting them home took long negotiation, and this National Security Archive posting examines one strange thread of it. Did President John F. Kennedy send Fidel Castro a secret warning through Brazil?

A warning routed through a third country would fit the odd diplomacy of the prisoner talks. Each side needed messages it could deny in public. The posting lays out the question and the evidence around it, and it shows how much of the rescue effort happened out of sight.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_environm:
In October 1986 a Soviet nuclear submarine carrying nuclear weapons sank north of Bermuda. Svetlana Savranskaya edited this briefing book, number 562, published on the thirtieth anniversary. Top secret minutes of a Politburo discussion anchor the record.

The minutes show Soviet leaders applying lessons from the Chernobyl disaster months earlier. Communication between Washington and Moscow about the accident stayed open. That openness came on the eve of the Reykjavik summit between Ronald Reagan and Mikhail Gorbachev. The documents catch two rivals handling a nuclear accident at sea with unusual candor, days before a meeting that nearly changed the arms race.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_intellig:
Area 51, the secret Nevada test site, became famous through the CIA's U-2 spy plane history, declassified in 2013. This briefing book, posted that October, argues the site's role was even larger. Documents show it served as a center for top secret stealth aircraft work in the 1970s and 1980s.

The site also hosted Soviet MiG fighters obtained in secret during the Cold War. American pilots could test their own aircraft against the real enemy machines. That double life, stealth development plus foreign fighter testing, makes Area 51 a genuine crossroads of intelligence and aviation history, beyond its flying-saucer fame.
hamlet: The most famous play in the world: Prince Hamlet of Denmark, grieving his father and disgusted by his mother's hasty marriage, feigns madness while plotting revenge. "To be, or not to be" is only one jewel in a play overflowing with them. Four hundred years on, it remains the deepest exploration of thought and action ever staged.
in-the-days-of-the-comet: H. G. Wells's In the Days of the Comet imagines a transformed human world. Gases from a green comet change man's nature in a single night. The narrator looks back calmly on the great change. Bold and visionary science fiction.
king-alfred-s-viking-a-story-of-the-firs:
King Alfred's Viking, a Story of the First English Fleet, is Charles W. Whistler's historical novel. Whistler's preface explains his sources: the details come from Asser's Life of Alfred. Alfred employed Norsemen whose names the record never gives. Whistler links them to Rolf the Ganger and Harald Fairhair's age.

He argues over battle sites with care, naming Ethandune and Kynwith and citing Bishop Clifford's identifications. Alfred's refuge at Athelney, the preface says, lies in scenes he could test himself. Whistler wrote many such tales of Saxon and Viking England. This one joins Alfred's fleet-building to a Norse hero's adventures. The preface shows a novelist checking chronicles like a scholar before daring his story.
lady-audley-s-secret:
Mary Elizabeth Braddon's Lady Audley's Secret is a famous sensation novel. Its first chapter, titled Lucy, opens at Audley Court. The house lies in a hollow of old timber and rich pasture.

A lime avenue, an old arch, and a one-handed clock set the mood. Lucy herself seems sweet, bright, and harmless. Yet the title promises a secret behind that fair surface. Braddon builds suspense from hidden identity and buried acts. The book helped define Victorian sensation fiction, a genre built on shocks and secrets. Robert Audley, the heroine's nephew by marriage, grows suspicious in time. His slow hunt for proof drives much of the suspense.
legend-of-moulin-huet:
Lizzie A. Freeth published her Legend of Moulin Huet at Guernsey in 1872. She had earlier written The Adventures of Carl Skinflint among the Fairies. Le Lievre printed the book at the Star Office there.

Freeth dedicated it to the Conway boys of the training ship Conway. She stresses that the story itself has no link to them. She simply owed that fine institution much gratitude, she says. The tale draws on Guernsey's own coastal lore. A mill, a bay, and local legend give the small book its charm. The Conway dedication shows Freeth's ties to naval families. Guernsey readers would know the Huet shore she describes.
lombard-street-a-description-of-the-mone:
Walter Bagehot describes London's money market in this famous essay. He names it Lombard Street to deal with concrete realities. Abstract words, he argues, falsely make the subject seem impalpable. Plain words can describe the market as clearly as anything.

Bagehot avoids Peel's Act of 1844 wherever possible. Controversy over that act caused half the supposed difficulty. When he must mention it, he stresses experienced effects only. Theory's refined basis interests him far less than practice. Few will attend to anything else once 1844 is mentioned, he warns. Experienced effects, not abstract theory, govern his treatment throughout.
maggie-miller-the-story-of-old-hagar-s-s:
Maggie Miller is a novel by Mary J. Holmes, subtitled Old Hagar's Secret. Holmes also wrote Lena Rivers and Tempest and Sunshine. Its motto is 'Lead us not into temptation.' The tale opens at the old house by the mill.

Hagar's secret hangs over Hester and the young Maggie. Girlhood, trifles, and expected guests fill the early chapters. Arthur Carrollton enters Maggie's life as the waters trouble. Madam Conway's disasters add comedy and social bite. Holmes was among America's best-selling novelists of her century. Her tales of love, class, and hidden birth thrilled millions. Maggie Miller is a fine sample of her sentimental art.
memoirs-of-the-court-of-louis-xiv-and-of:
Elizabeth Charlotte of Bavaria, Duchesse d'Orleans, wrote the memoirs in this set. She was mother of the Regent, as the title page states. Her letters to kin across Europe ran to near eight hundred.

A Brunswick councillor, De Praun, picked the best parts after her death. The first printed set, in 1788, was cut and weakened by censors. Names were struck out, and her bold German turns were softened. This complete set restores the extracts with life and force intact. A life of the princess in a later reprint read like a sermon. This set aims to keep her salt and salt alone.
montlivet:
Alice Prescott Smith published this frontier novel with Grosset and Dunlap in 1907. Its contents begin with a key, a captive, and a scene behind the commandant's door. The action moves into an Ottawa camp, then westward toward the islands. A character named Mary Starling enters midway, and a compact is made.

Later chapters gather over Cadillac's table and in council. Cadillac founded Detroit, and the novel breathes that French Great Lakes world. Storms, mist, and mixed motives fill the middle chapters. Smith writes a romance of the old Northwest, where French officers, traders, and Native nations bargain and fight over the lakes country.
moonfleet:
J. Meade Falkner published this Dorset adventure in 1898. He dedicates it to all Mohunes of Fleet and Moonfleet, living or dead. The contents open in Moonfleet village, with floods and a discovery. A vault, a rescue, and an assault follow in quick succession.

Later chapters bring an auction, a landing, and a judgment. A sea-cave, a funeral, and a well-house deepen the danger. The last named chapters are The Well and The Jewel. Smugglers and a cursed diamond drive the tale. Generations of readers have ranked it among the finest adventure stories in English.
mr-marx-s-secret:
E. Phillips Oppenheim wrote this mystery novel, first issued in 1899 and reprinted in 1916. The title page lists his other tales of intrigue. Chapter one is called News from the Pacific. A frontispiece shows a man vowing to end a beast's misery.

Oppenheim builds the plot around a secret held by Mr. Marx. News, travel, and hidden motives drive the early chapters. His style favors short scenes, talk, and sudden turns. Readers follow who knows the secret and who wants it. The book is an early sample of the spy and crime tales that made Oppenheim famous.
nan-sherwood-at-pine-camp-or-the-old-lum:
Annie Roe Carr sends Nan Sherwood to a winter lumber camp here. Chapter one opens on High Street in Tillbury, by the high school. Bess Harley spots a crowd at the Atwater Mills gate. Nan's merry face clouds at once at the sight.

Nan is rosy-cheeked, brown-eyed, and hard to keep still in class. Yet she is no thoughtless girl, the narrator insists. Trouble at the mill starts her trip to Pine Camp. An old lumberman's secret waits in the snowbound woods. V1 promises snow fun, new friends, and a light mystery, in cheerful series fiction for girls.
nasa-tm-19650025650-analytic-solutions-t:
Richard S Brokaw at Lewis Research Center worked out exact, analytic solutions for how a hydrogen and oxygen mixture ignites. The paper was prepared for a combustion meeting at Cambridge in England in August 1964. Ignition kinetics is the study of the chain of chemical steps that leads to burning. Hydrogen and oxygen react with explosive speed once lit.

Analytic solutions give insight that pure number work cannot. They show which steps control the delay before ignition. Rocket engines burn these same gases, so the timing of ignition matters for safe starts. Brokaw's solutions gave combustion scientists a clean base for checking both theory and engine practice.
nasa-tm-19670002044-the-effects-of-space:
Frederick Gordon Jr. and Harry E. Wannemacher Jr., of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, wrote this report in August 1966. It studies what space radiation does to MOSFET transistors, and what those effects mean for engineers who build with them. Goddard was then putting metal-oxide-semiconductor circuits into spacecraft telemetry systems.

The introduction explains why Goddard chose these devices despite the radiation risk. They saved so much size and power that no rival circuit class could do the same job. Bipolar circuits met the space limits but missed the power limits by a wide margin. Conventional parts met the power limits but not the space limits. The first spacecraft set to fly the devices were the IMP-D and IMP-F satellites, whose orbits would expose them to harsh radiation.
nasa-tm-19670008546-simultaneous-trapped:
Donald J. Williams and Norman F. Ness, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, wrote this paper in June 1966. Using satellite data, it watches two things at once. First come energetic electrons trapped in Earth's radiation belts, and the magnetic field in Earth's long magnetic tail. That tail stretches away from the Sun.

Data from the polar-orbiting satellite 1963 38C tracked the high-latitude trapping boundary at 1,100 kilometers from March 15 through June 3, 1964. At the onset of magnetic storms, that boundary suddenly collapsed toward lower latitudes. Meanwhile the IMP-1 satellite measured field strength inside the tail itself. Comparing the two records, three cases matched the latitude drops predicted by an extended tail shape, and one did not. The authors call the results direct evidence that the tail field governs trapped particles in quiet times and storms alike.
nasa-tm-19670014616-rare-earth-analysis-:
C. C. Schnetzler, H. H. Thomas, and John A. Philpotts, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, wrote this analysis paper. It presents a new way to measure rare-earth elements in rocks and minerals. The method uses a mass spectrometer with stable isotope dilution. A sample is spiked with known amounts of chosen isotopes to reveal the abundances present.

The technique was already in routine use for europium and the seven even-numbered rare-earth elements. That set, the authors say, is enough to outline the general rare-earth abundance pattern of a rock. Results matched neutron activation analysis in quality, or beat it, while running faster and more simply. As a check, the team determined rare-earth abundances in two standard rocks, known as W-1 and G-1, whose values other laboratories could compare against.
nasa-tm-19680008597-propulsive-potential:
Joseph L. Ansell, of the Delta Project Office at Goddard Space Flight Center, wrote this paper in February 1968. It assesses the propulsive potential of residual rocket motor heat. A spent solid rocket motor stays hot after burnout. Ansell asks whether that leftover heat can still do useful work in vacuum.

His scheme sprays an inert quenching fluid into the hot motor, flashing it to gas that escapes as thrust. Three fluids were compared, water, propane, and Freon 12, applied to the Delta launch vehicle's third stage motors. Water proved superior under the conditions assumed. The method appears feasible, the study finds, for fine velocity trimming within six minutes after burnout. A computer program predicts the effect of introducing the quenching fluid at various times after the motor's peak temperature. Planners can thus pick the best moment.
nasa-tm-19700013645-marshall-space-fligh:
William M. Greene of the Space Sciences Laboratory at the Marshall Space Flight Center wrote this report on April 15, 1969. It covers the gravity network set up around the center in Huntsville, Alabama. That network supported work on a laser instrument meant to measure gravity with great exactness.

Greene made early field seismic measurements at seven proposed sites in and around Redstone Arsenal. He also set out a local gravity net and a wider one across the state to meet test needs. Every result, he reports, pointed the same way: the instrument site needed shielding from ground vibration. The work ended with an optimum permanent field site chosen for the tests.
nasa-tm-19710018232-experiments-on-the-e:
NASA preprint X-322-71-165 reports experiments on ultraviolet light and contamination inside vacuum systems; the author's name is poorly rendered in the scan. Thin films of stray material can coat hardware inside vacuum chambers and spoil sensitive tests. The experiments ran in an otherwise empty chamber and watched the films with a quartz crystal microbalance.

Data from the microbalance showed that ultraviolet light changes what clean and contaminated even mean inside a chamber. The chamber's past use mattered most, far more than the pumping mechanism. Under ultraviolet exposure, a chamber with a dirty history behaved differently from a clean one. The report recommends checking for contamination with ultraviolet irradiation whenever an experiment is critical.
navajo-silversmiths-second-annual-report:
Washington Matthews, a United States Army doctor, wrote Navajo Silversmiths for the Smithsonian's Bureau of Ethnology. The piece ran in the bureau's second annual report, for 1880 to 1881, printed in Washington in 1883. Plates show silver objects, a workshop, crucibles, and stone molds.

Matthews says many Navajo smiths work chiefly in silver, though some forge iron and brass. He could not learn when or how the art began among them. Some held that it did not come from Europeans at all. He notes that tools from American and Mexican traders had shaped the craft, and that the work had improved in recent years.
o-flaherty-v-c-a-recruiting-pamphlet:
George Bernard Shaw wrote O'Flaherty V. C. as a recruiting pamphlet in play form. In 1915, he says, this little play was a recruiting poster in disguise. British officers seldom like Irish soldiers, he begins, yet always try to keep a share of them in a battalion. Irish dash, he argues, gives impetus to bold operations.

Irish recruiting in 1915 was badly bungled, Shaw charges. Irishmen were mostly Roman Catholics and loyal Irishmen, which English eyes read as heretics and rebels. Yet they were willing to soldier beside France and see the world. The War Office, he says, approached them from Dublin Castle's view, not their own. Commissions denied to Catholic officers repulsed them.
one-basket:
Edna Ferber gathered thirty-one short stories in this book. An introduction opens the collection for readers. The first tale is The Woman Who Tried to Be Good. It is dated 1913 in the table of contents. Blanche Devine owns the House with the Closed Shutters.

Blanche trails fine clothes down Main Street in the tale. No man lifts his hat, and no woman bows. Storekeepers overcharge her, and she pays in silence. She has no redress as a woman of her class. Ferber writes with pity for judged and lonely people. Her tales mix humor, pathos, and small-town life.
pinocchio-the-tale-of-a-puppet:
Carlo Collodi's Pinocchio: The Tale of a Puppet is the story of a wooden puppet who laughs and cries like a child and wants to become a real boy. This edition, illustrated by Alice Carsey, was published by the Whitman Publishing Company of Racine, Wisconsin, in 1916.

The first chapter asks how a piece of wood could laugh and cry like a child, and from there Pinocchio runs through one scrape after another. He is famous for the nose that grows when he lies, and for learning, slowly and painfully, to be good. Generations of children have met him first in some edition like this one.
poems-and-ballads-third-series-taken-fro:
Algernon Charles Swinburne's Poems and Ballads, Third Series, appears here as taken from the third volume of his collected poetical works, published by William Heinemann in London. Swinburne was the most musical and provocative English poet of his generation, famous for verse that celebrated pagan feeling and challenged Victorian respectability. The collected edition arranged his output across six volumes, from the first Poems and Ballads through songs, roundels, and dramatic poems.

Within that scheme the third series continues the ballad and lyric work that made his reputation, full of the rushing metres and rich sound that readers either loved or condemned. Placed beside the second series and the Songs of the Springtides in the same collected volume, it shows Swinburne in his mature manner. Readers who want the poet whole rather than in selections can follow his career volume by volume here.
rip-foster-in-ride-the-gray-planet:
Blake Savage wrote this Golden Griffon space adventure for boys, copyrighted in 1952 by Western Publishing Company. Golden Press of New York issued the first Golden Griffon printing in 1969. Rip Foster is its hero, and the fourteen chapter titles promise a fast ride through peril in space.

Spacebound and Rake That Radiation open the tale, followed by Capture and Drive and Find the Needle. The Gray World and Rip's Planet give the mission its ground, and Earthbound turns the course homeward. Duck — or Die, Repel Invaders, and Get the Scorpion raise the fighting pitch. Mercury Transit, Peril, and Between Two Fires close the list.
romeo-and-juliet:
William Shakespeare's tragedy of Romeo and Juliet is set out here by acts and scenes, with a list of its persons. Escalus, Prince of Verona, heads that list, with Mercutio, the Prince's kinsman and Romeo's friend, and Paris, a young nobleman, after him. A chorus speaks the prologue and returns in the second act.

The scenes move from a public place and a street to rooms and a hall in Capulet's house, and to Capulet's garden by night. Friar Lawrence's cell recurs through the middle acts. The last act shifts to a street in Mantua and ends in a churchyard, in a monument belonging to the Capulets, where the lovers' story closes.
ruth-fielding-of-the-red-mill-or-jasper-:
Alice B. Emerson's Ruth Fielding of the Red Mill, or Jasper Parloe's Secret, is headed with the year 1913. Chapter I, The Red Flame in the Night, opens with the sound of drumming wheels roaring in Ruth's ears for hours. She sits in the last car of the afternoon Limited, whirling from the West to the East through the rich valleys of Upper New York State. Cheslow is not many miles ahead now. She has found it on the railroad timetable and on the map printed on the back of the sheet, and she has spelled out station names with quick eyes until dusk fell.

Ruth is glad to have a seat to herself, since a seatmate might have seen how hard she works to keep back tears. She is by no means one of the crying kind, she insists, and she had banned tears for this occasion weeks ago.
somerset: G. W. Wade and J. H. Wade wrote Somerset. Methuen and Co. printed the London book. It holds thirty-two pictures and two maps. One picture maps the railways of Somerset. An other shows the Pinnacles at Cheddar. The contents open with an introduction in nine heads. They treat the county's lie and reach. Weather and links by road and rail follow. Land shape, rocks, beasts, and plants come next. The past, old remains, trades, and famed folk close the list.
the-alchemist-s-secret:
Isabel Cecilia Williams wrote The Alchemist's Secret, a set of tales printed by P. J. Kenedy and Sons of New York with rights held in 1910. Eleven tales are listed, from The Passing of Tony and The Tramp through Nancy's Tale, Patsy, The Story of Julie Benoit, and God's Way.

The Passing of Tony opens at a small post office, where Tony asks Widow Bascomb if the last mail is in and if it holds a thing for him that night. She knows full well it does not, yet she still turns to the letters in their pigeonhole to check for him. Her sour face and rasping voice soften as she smiles on the lad. Readers get warm, faith-touched tales of poor folk, priests, and small mercies.
the-amulet:
Hendrik Conscience builds The Amulet on an event said to have happened at Antwerp in the sixteenth century. The title page names him as author of The Lion of Flanders, The Conscript, Blind Rosa, and many more tales. The English here was made, the title page states, expressly for this edition. A translator signs the preface with the initials S. J. F. from Baltimore.

That preface calls the tale one of a dark and bloody deed met by swift and dreadful payback. Crafty plots fall apart, it argues, when heaven's justice brings them to light. Good acts, by contrast, bear fruit in this world and shield a person from foes. The first chapter is headed simply Antwerp.
the-anti-slavery-alphabet:
Printed at Philadelphia for the Anti-Slavery Fair in 1847 by Merrihew and Thompson, this small book teaches children the case against slavery letter by letter. A verse at the front speaks to little readers directly. They are young, it admits, but there is much they can do.

Children can plead with grown men not to buy slaves again and to free those they hold. They can talk with playmates on the walk from school about the slave child, motherless and alone. They can refuse candy and cake not made by free hands. The alphabet then begins: A is an abolitionist, and each letter carries its own short lesson in the cause.
the-brighton-boys-with-the-submarine-fle:
Lieutenant James R. Driscoll wrote The Brighton Boys with the Submarine Fleet. Its twenty-six chapters run from Good-by, Brighton and Down in a Submarine to sealed orders in the North Sea. German raiders, a ramming by a destroyer, and a mine field come early. A rescue, fog, Yankee camouflage, and life on the bottom of the sea fill the mid heads. Capturing a U-Boat, a trap, chlorine gas, and the Stars and Stripes close the list.

The tale opens on Jack Hammond, reading a newspaper spread over his knees. Bold type calls for young men to enlist in Uncle Sam's submarine fleet for service in European waters. A great force of young Americans is wanted to man the undersea ships to be sent abroad against Germany. Stirred by the appeal, Jack pulls the paper closer and reads each word.
the-case-of-the-golden-bullet:
The Case of the Golden Bullet is by Grace Isabel Colbron and Augusta Groner. It opens not with the case but with an introduction to Joe Muller. Muller is a secret service detective of the Imperial Austrian police. Muller is a small, slight, plain-looking man of indefinite age and humble manner, nothing like the impressive Holmes or the brilliant Lecoq.

The introduction explains that humility. In early youth a miscarriage of justice gave him years in prison. The stigma barred him from honest employment afterward. That threw him back on his peculiar talents. It drove him into the police. Red tape keeps his official rank barely above a policeman's, though kings and councillors consult him, and his modesty asks for nothing but a sufficient income and work he enjoys.
the-chaplain-of-the-fleet: Walter Besant and James Rice wrote this novel together, dated 1881 in its heading. Only the title page and the contents of Part I, headed Within the Rules, are present here. The chapter titles follow a girl named Kitty, who loses her father and her friends, makes engagements, rides to London by coach, first sees the doctor, and witnesses a fleet wedding.The book itself never opens here.
the-chequers-being-the-natural-history-o: James Runciman, author of Skippers and Shellbacks, edited this record, subtitled the natural history of a public house set forth in a loafer's diary, published in London by Ward and Downey. Only the title page, dedication, and the start of the contents are present here. The dedication, addressed to Philip Wood and John Wood of South Shields, calls the book a record of ruined lives. It thanks them for the writer's training from age seventeen in their house, and for their good relations with the police. No diary text follows.
the-figure-in-the-carpet:
Henry James wrote The Figure in the Carpet as a tale of books and the men who read them, printed at London in 1916 from the final text. A young critic tells the tale in his own voice.

The critic recalls the night George Corvick begged him to review a new novel by Hugh Vereker for their paper. He seized the chance, since he would soon meet Vereker at a country house. Praise, pride, and a hunt for the one secret plan said to hide in all Vereker's work drive the tale. James turns a book review into a quiet study of fame and blind spots.
the-forsyte-saga-volume-iii-awakening-to: John Galsworthy wrote Awakening and To Let as volume three of The Forsyte Saga. This copy's heading dates it 1926. Only the front matter and start of contents are present here. The heads name a meeting and a fine fleur Forsyte. They name Robin Hill, a mausoleum, and the native heath. Figures called Jon and Fleur appear. Parts for mothers and sons and for fathers and daughters follow. No page of the tale itself is included in this portion.
the-great-secret: E. Phillips Oppenheim wrote The Great Secret. A heading dates the book 1906. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page and a contents list of eighteen chapters. The heads open with Room No. 317 and A Midnight Raid. They name Miss Van Hoyt and A Match at Lord's. They name the mysterious Mr. Guest and Wortley Foote, the spy. Later heads name A Legacy of Danger, Gathering Jackals, and A Dying Man. They name Nagaski's Instinct. They end with In the Death Chamber. No chapter text is present.
the-last-chronicle-of-barset: Anthony Trollope closed his Barsetshire series with a novel first issued in monthly parts from December 1866 to July 1867. Only the front pages and contents are present here, listing early chapters on Mr. Crawley before the magistrates, Grace Crawley, the archdeacon threat, and dinner at Framley Court. The novel itself, with Crawley cheque trouble and the Proudie household, does not appear in this record beyond those chapter titles.
the-little-nugget: P. G. Wodehouse's early comic novel centers on Ogden Ford — the Little Nugget — a monstrously spoiled child heir whom various parties plot to kidnap. Enter Sam Fisher, tutor and reluctant schemer, in a tangle of abductions and romance. The master's light touch is already evident in this fast, funny romp.
the-net: Rex Beach, the bestselling author of The Spoilers, spins a novel of intrigue and high-stakes scheming. His hero is drawn into a web of plotters where money, power, and a woman's honor hang in the balance. Beach's muscular, fast-moving style made him one of America's most popular storytellers, and this tale delivers the adventure his readers expected.
the-outlet: Andy Adams's 1905 Western about the outlet: a cattle drive up the trail, told by a real cowboy. Authentic and vivid, it is the classic of the trail. The West as it truly was. Adams lived the trail he describes.
the-phoenix-and-the-carpet: E. Nesbit's 1904 fantasy about children who find an egg that hatches into a vain, talkative Phoenix, plus a magic carpet for adventures. Their wishes go wonderfully wrong in episodes both funny and touching. Lighter than her time-travel books but just as inventive, it is pure childhood joy in story form.
the-silent-bullet: Arthur Reeve’s Craig Kennedy mysteries: the silent bullet and other cases solved by science. The American Sherlock applies the laboratory to crime, ingenious and very much of the 1910s. His science was as modern as tomorrow.
the-stokesley-secret: The Stokesley Secret, Charlotte Yonge's children's tale. The children's secret. This book preserves that story. The paper lived through the years. Tomorrow's readers will find it. Its place in history is secure. The archive guards it with care.
the-story-of-the-amulet: E. Nesbit's 1906 fantasy in which the Bastable-style children find half of an ancient Egyptian amulet and travel through time to find the other half. Ancient Babylon, Caesar's Britain, and a utopian future flash past in thrilling episodes. The most ambitious of Nesbit's fantasies, it blends history, magic, and humor into a children's classic.
the-white-gauntlet: The White Gauntlet, Mayne Reid's tale. The gauntlet's challenge. This book preserves that western. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
to-let: Galsworthy's To Let closes an era for the long Forsyte chronicle. The old family faces change, loss, and the modern age. The 1921 novel mourns a passing England. The Forsyte Saga's poignant and fitting finale to a great chronicle.
zweig-the-burning-secret:
At an Austrian resort, a suave baron befriends a lonely twelve-year-old boy as a path to the boy's mother. Stefan Zweig's The Burning Secret, from 1911 and presented here in English, turns on the moment the child understands the game. Jealousy and betrayal follow, and innocence ends in a single burning insight.

Zweig tells the story from inside the boy's awakening mind with unbearable precision. The mother's romance, the baron's polish, and the child's fury interlock like gears. Few novellas anywhere study childhood's end so exactly. The Burning Secret made Zweig's early reputation across Europe. It still reads as a small masterpiece of psychological fiction, perfectly paced to its final reconciliation.
